sentences.text: This genus belongs to the group of ancient apodiform birds.
Their physical appearance closely resembled that of today's treeswifts.
They possessed wings shaped like sickles, a feature seen in modern swifts.
Although they are not direct ancestors of modern swifts, they kept a basic body structure.
Richard Lydekker first described this genus in the year 1891.
These birds formed their own distinct family called the Aegialornithidae.
It remains uncertain which other genera should be placed within this family.
The placement of the genus Cypselavus is debated, as it might be an aegialornithid or a treeswift.
Including the Jungornithidae family in the Aegialornithidae is a controversial idea.
Remains of these birds date from the Early to Late Eocene epoch.
Scientists estimate their time range falls between 41.03 and 37.71 million years ago.
Fossils have been discovered in Middle to Late Eocene layers in Germany and France.
Researchers question if an Early Eocene record from the Nanjemoy Formation in Virginia belongs to Aegialornis, since apodiform birds may not have existed there until after the Eocene.
The taxonomy of Aegialornis species is debated, with some researchers considering A. germanicus and A. leenhardti as junior synonyms of A. gallicus.
It is debated whether A. broweri is based on small individuals of A. wetmorei, and the proposal to separate them into the genus Mesogiornis has not found general acceptance.
